01 — Overview

How this mechanism works, in general. Read this before you write code; it is deliberately free of implementation detail.

Why this is chapter one

Every harness is a loop around a function that talks to a model. That function is the only part of the system that is not yours: it fails on someone else's schedule, costs money per call, answers differently every time, and is impossible to test.

So you put a seam around it on day one. Not as a design flourish — as the thing that makes the next ten chapters gradable at all.

   yours: deterministic                │  not yours: random, slow, paid
   ────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────
   loop → tools → session → provider ──┼──▶ model ──▶ back through provider

Above the seam you can assert anything. Below it, nothing. So the first thing you build is the seam, and the first thing you learn is what crosses it.

What actually crosses the seam

Not "a prompt". A structure. An OpenAI-compatible request is a model name, an ordered list of messages with roles, and optionally a list of tool definitions:

Request
├── model        "gpt-4o-mini"
├── messages     [ {system, "..."}, {user, "..."} ]
├── tools        []            ← empty in this chapter
└── stream       true

The response is not a structure. It is a sequence of partial structures, and reassembling it is the chapter.

Why the wire is a stream

Two reasons, and only the second is obvious.

  1. Latency. The user sees the first token in ~200 ms instead of waiting for

the whole answer.

  1. Length. A response can be longer than any single HTTP chunk can

comfortably carry, and the server does not know in advance how long it will be.

So the server emits text/event-stream: a plain-text framing of "here is a bit more". Each bit is a JSON object with a delta, meaning "the part that is new".

   request ──────────────────────────────▶
                                            (server builds the answer
                                             one token at a time)
   ◀──── data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"The "}}]}    ← chunk 1
   ◀──── data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"quick "}}]}  ← chunk 2
   ◀──── data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"fox."}}]}    ← chunk 3
   ◀──── data: {...,"usage":{...}}                          ← chunk 4
   ◀──── data: [DONE]                                       ← terminator

The delta is nested twice: one chunk can carry several choices, and each choice carries its own delta. That nesting is the part people get wrong from memory, so here is the exact shape to decode into:

{
  "choices": [
    { "index": 0, "delta": { "content": "The " }, "finish_reason": null }
  ],
  "usage": { "prompt_tokens": 42, "completion_tokens": 7, "total_tokens": 49 }
}

The choices array exists because a request can ask for several completions. This course asks for one, sends no n, and folds choices[0]. A stream with more than one choice would interleave alternatives, and folding them all would concatenate them.

The mental model to hold: the stream is a delta log, and your job is to fold it. Every chunk is an event, not a document. Nothing in the stream is the complete answer; the complete answer is what you get by applying all the deltas in order.

Once you see it that way, three properties stop being trivia and become obvious:

  • Append, never assign. Folding is an accumulation.
  • Metadata arrives late. Usage is only known once the server has finished

producing the answer, so it rides on the final chunk, whose delta is empty.

  • The terminator is not data. [DONE] is framing, not a message.

Why the failure modes cluster here

A provider client has an unusually bad ratio of code to failure modes, because it sits on a network boundary with three independent clocks: yours, the server's, and the connection's.

Each branch is a graded case, and each one has a plausible-looking wrong implementation:

BranchThe wrong implementationThe case
non-2xxdecode the error body as a completionhttp-error
stream diesignore scanner.Err()truncated-stream
deltasassign instead of appendprints-reply
shaperead delta from the top level instead of choices[0].deltaprints-reply, sse-framing
metadataonly decode chunks that carry contentdebug-usage
requestforget stream: true, or build the URL by handrequest-shape, request-envelope
lifetimeuse context.Background() instead of ctxrequest-timeout

That last one deserves a note: context.Background() works. The request succeeds. It only fails when someone tries to cancel you — which is exactly what chapter 08 (steering and abort) does, and by then the bug is three chapters old and invisible.

Why the scripted server is not a cheat

It would be easy to think "they gave me a fake server, so I'm not really talking to a model". The opposite is true.

internal/fake is a real HTTP server. It binds a socket, parses your request, validates your headers, and writes real SSE bytes with real chunk boundaries and a real [DONE]. The only thing replaced is the content of the reply — which is the one thing a test can never control and never needs to. When you point this same client at Ollama and it works, nothing changes but the base URL, because the protocol was the protocol.

This is the course's central trick, stated plainly: replace the model, keep the wire. That is how every harness in the world tests itself, and you will do it again for tools, sessions, and subagents.
